headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: RD-Agent can read/write logs and use browsers/APIs, while Semantic Kernel can read/write application-defined files and use MCP servers. That creates a plausible shared-content bridge where attacker-controlled content from A can reach B’s tool prompts. No direct provenance controls are documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF A writes untrusted web or dataset content into shared files that B later reads
IF B forwards file content into prompts or MCP tool calls without provenance filtering
mitigations: Separate A and B into different workspaces
Disable automatic file ingestion in B
Add a provenance tag to every file passed from A to B
Review browser-sourced content before B consumes it
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization and allowlists at the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, and logs, and has broad network egress plus API access. B reads and writes filesystem content and also has broad egress. If they share a workspace or memory store, sensitive A data can flow into B and then out to third-party APIs, making leakage materially plausible.
conditions: IF A and B share any filesystem, memory store, or mounted workspace
IF B sends read file contents to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face/MCP tools
mitigations: Place A and B in separate storage volumes
Remove sensitive datasets from any shared path
Restrict B’s outbound API destinations
Rotate any secrets exposed in shared logs
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls and DLP scanning

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A supports multiple instances and writes logs; B supports multiple instances, writes files, and shares state via memory store. Even though B cannot modify git state or spawn subprocesses, overlapping write surfaces on shared mutable resources can still race or overwrite each other in default multi-instance setups.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or memory store
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking or per-instance namespaces
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories
Namespace shared memory keys by agent
Serialize writes with a lock file
Check for stale outputs before overwrite
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a research agent that can browse and call APIs; B is a kernel-plus-plugins orchestrator that can route outputs into tools. If B treats A’s generated research, facts, or citations as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s outputs as final facts without a verification step
IF B uses those outputs to trigger plugin or API actions
mitigations: Require a human review step for A’s outputs
Add citation checks before B acts
Compare A’s claims against a second source
Log and flag low-confidence outputs
requires-engineering: implement structured verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly touches financial reports and competition datasets, while B handles application context and can send data to external model providers or MCP servers. The profiles do not document residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. I cite both because the risk arises from A’s sensitive data flowing through B’s externalized tooling.
conditions: IF A’s financial or competition data is processed through B’s external model providers
IF the deployment has residency, retention, or DPA requirements not enforced by the orchestrator
mitigations: Classify A’s inputs before routing to B
Block regulated data from external APIs
Document retention settings for each provider
Use region-locked endpoints where available
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
